notes.meaning: Jesus and His followers reached the villages on the Mount of Olives near Jerusalem. This was the final part of His journey toward the cross. From there, Jesus sent two disciples ahead with special instructions.

Jesus told the two disciples to find a young donkey tied near the village entrance and bring it to Him. Animals chosen for sacred tasks had never been ridden or worked before. If anyone questioned them, they were to explain that the Lord needed it and would return it quickly.

The disciples went into the village and found the young donkey tied by an outside doorway on the street. Some bystanders asked why they were taking it. The disciples gave Jesus' exact message, and the owners let them take the animal.

The disciples brought the young donkey to Jesus and laid their outer cloaks on its back as a makeshift saddle. Jesus then sat upon it to ride into the city. By riding a gentle donkey instead of a war horse, He showed He was the peaceful King promised by the prophets.

The crowds welcomed Jesus by laying their garments along the road in front of Him. Others spread out leafy branches they had gathered from nearby fields. This was a special honor given to welcome a king or victor.

Crowds walking ahead and behind Jesus praised God with shouts from the Psalms. The word Hosanna was an expression of deep joy that originally meant 'save now.' They celebrated Jesus as the ruler coming in God's name to restore the royal kingdom promised to King David.

Jesus entered Jerusalem and walked into the outer courts of the temple. He looked closely at everything happening there, inspecting the worship space. Because it was already late in the day, He left the city to sleep in Bethany with the twelve disciples.

The next morning, Jesus and His disciples walked back toward Jerusalem from Bethany. Jesus became hungry as they traveled. His hunger shows His full humanity as He began another busy day of public ministry.

Jesus saw a fig tree with green leaves and walked over to see if it held any fruit. Fig trees usually put out small edible buds before or along with their leaves. Because it only had leaves and no fruit, it showed plenty of outward promise but had nothing real to offer.

differ.view: Some Baptists saw the tree's season as a picture of people who produce no fruit until God calls them by His powerful grace.
Early Methodists explained that this phrase simply meant it was an unfavorable year for the early fig crop.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching often sees this act as a living parable announcing the end of the old temple worship and a warning against offering God empty excuses.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern commentators view cursing a tree for lacking ripe fruit out of season as surprising or difficult to justify on a literal level.

notes.meaning: Jesus spoke directly to the tree and declared that no one would ever eat fruit from it again. The disciples heard what He said and noted the solemn command. This miracle was a prophetic action pointing to the coming judgment on religious hypocrisy.

When Jesus reached the temple in Jerusalem, He drove out the merchants and customers who had set up shop in the courtyards. He flipped over the tables of those exchanging foreign coins and knocked over the seats of men selling sacrificial birds. The temple leaders had permitted business and profiteering inside God's holy courts.

Jesus stopped people from carrying everyday equipment and goods across the temple grounds. People were using the sacred courtyards as a noisy shortcut between different areas of the city. He demanded that proper reverence be restored to the place dedicated to God.

Jesus taught the crowd by quoting the prophets Isaiah and Jeremiah to defend His actions. The temple court was intended as a place where people from all foreign nations could draw near to worship God. Instead, dishonest leaders had crowded them out and turned the space into a hideout for thieves.

The leading priests and religious teachers heard what Jesus said and began looking for a way to have Him put to death. They felt threatened because the ordinary crowds were captivated by His bold teaching. Their fear of His popularity kept them from arresting Him openly right away.

When evening arrived, Jesus and the disciples left the city of Jerusalem. They went back out to the countryside, likely staying the night in the village of Bethany. This daily routine kept Him safe from secret nighttime attacks by His opponents.

Walking past the fig tree early the following morning, the disciples noticed that it was completely dead all the way down to its roots. Peter remembered Jesus' words and pointed out how fast the tree had withered away. The sudden death of the plant showed the divine power backing Jesus' words.

Jesus answered Peter by telling the disciples to place their whole trust in God. True faith does not look at human strength, but relies completely on God's unlimited power. He used the dried-up tree to direct their hearts to the Lord as the source of all spiritual help.

differ.view: Some Holiness teachers read this as a second, perfect faith that completely excludes doubt, given during entire sanctification.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The traditional Catholic Douay-Rheims version translates the phrase literally as 'Have the faith of God.'

notes.meaning: Jesus said that whoever commands an enormous obstacle like a mountain to plunge into the sea without doubting in their heart will see it happen. In Jewish speech, a mountain meant an impossible barrier or severe problem. God removes the greatest difficulties when His servants step forward in genuine faith.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Word of Faith teachers understand this verse to teach that spoken words possess creative power to bring physical health and material wealth into being.

notes.meaning: Jesus encouraged the disciples to pray with full confidence that God hears and answers them. Believers are told to trust so thoroughly in God's willingness to give that they view the answer as already granted. This bold confidence rests on God's goodness and His revealed promises.

differ.view: Reformed teachers emphasize that this promise applies only to things aligned with God's revealed will, rejecting any claim that believers can demand whatever they want.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Prosperity preachers often present this passage as a blank check guaranteeing that mental belief will deliver whatever earthly blessings someone asks for.

notes.meaning: Whenever believers stand to pray, they must freely forgive anyone who has wronged them. An angry and bitter spirit shuts the door on genuine fellowship with God. Our heavenly Father expects those who receive His mercy to show that same mercy to others.

If people refuse to let go of their grudges, their heavenly Father will not pardon their own sins. A closed heart that holds on to bitterness proves it does not truly understand divine forgiveness. God's mercy must transform how we treat the people around us.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Modern textual scholars note that this verse is absent from the oldest and best Greek manuscripts and was likely added later from Matthew 6:15.

notes.meaning: Back inside the temple courts, a delegation of chief priests, scribes, and elders confronted Jesus. These groups made up the ruling council of the nation and demanded to know who gave Him the right to cleanse the courts and teach. Because they did not authorize Him, they challenged His divine commission.

Jesus agreed to answer their challenge if they would first resolve one question for Him. He asked whether John the Baptist received his ministry from God in heaven or from human invention. Demanding a direct reply, Jesus exposed the true state of their hearts.

The leaders huddled together to discuss how to escape the trap. If they confessed that John was sent by God, Jesus would ask why they did not believe his testimony. But if they called John a fraud, they feared the crowd would turn violent because the common people were convinced John was a true prophet.

To protect their standing, the religious leaders gave the dishonest answer that they did not know. Since they refused to acknowledge the truth about John, Jesus declined to tell them where His own authority came from. People who close their eyes to God's obvious truth forfeit any right to further instruction.
